edges.description: Cortical TDP-43, tau, or Alzheimer pathology drives asymmetric neuronal loss and focal cortical atrophy in left-hemisphere language regions.
edges.source: Cortical Proteinopathy Accumulation in Language Regions

edges.description: Focal cortical neuronal degeneration is accompanied by axonal degeneration along the dorsal (superior longitudinal fasciculus) and ventral (inferior longitudinal and uncinate fasciculi) language pathways.
edges.target: Dorsal and Ventral White Matter Language Tract Disconnection

edges.description: Focal left-hemisphere cortical atrophy and synaptic loss directly degrade regional metabolic activity and function across the distributed language network.
Structural disconnection of dorsal and ventral white matter bundles correlates directly with impaired lexical retrieval and compounds cortical atrophy to produce network-level language dysfunction.
edges.source: Dorsal and Ventral White Matter Language Tract Disconnection

edges.description: Degeneration of the language network is what produces the progressive, initially isolated loss of language function that defines the syndrome; the isolation of the deficit is what distinguishes it from the other frontotemporal dementia syndromes at onset.
Disruption of left-hemisphere lexical-semantic and phonological retrieval networks produces early, persistent naming impairment across all three canonical PPA variants.

Degeneration of the left posterior frontoinsular cortex and dorsal language stream in nonfluent/agrammatic PPA impairs syntactic encoding and speech fluency, producing agrammatism and effortful, halting speech.
Anterior temporal language-network degeneration in semantic variant PPA erodes lexical-semantic representations, causing progressive single-word comprehension loss.
Loss of irregular-word lexical-semantic representations in semantic variant PPA forces reliance on sublexical phonological decoding, producing surface dyslexia.

Degeneration of the left posterior temporoparietal phonological loop in logopenic variant PPA impairs phonological short-term memory, causing deficits in sentence and phrase repetition alongside word-retrieval pauses.
Involvement of left posterior frontoinsular speech-motor planning regions in agrammatic/nonfluent PPA (especially 4R-tauopathy cases) produces concurrent apraxia of speech.

Behavioural involvement is a later consequence of the same degenerative process rather than a parallel one: the diagnostic criteria require language to remain isolated for at least two years, and behaviour is named among the domains the disease progresses into. The edge is marked indirect because the entry does not model that spread as a node of its own.
intermediate_mechanisms: Degeneration spreads beyond the language network as the disease progresses, recruiting behaviour, executive function and judgment.

nodes.description: Agrammatism in spoken or written language production and/or labored, effortful, halting speech with syntactic comprehension impairment for complex sentences, defining nonfluent/agrammatic variant PPA.

evidence.reference_title: Language training for oral and written naming impairment in primary progressive aphasia: a review.
evidence.snippet: nf/avPPA has main clinical features of agrammatism in language production and/or effortful halting speech [6].

evidence.reference_title: A review on primary progressive aphasia.
evidence.snippet: The agrammatic subtype, which is similar to the Neary et al (1998) criteria for the PNFA subtype of FTLD, is characterized by labored speech, agrammatism in production and/or comprehension, variable degrees of anomia, and phonemic paraphasias, in the presence of relatively normal word comprehension.

nodes.description: Early, persistent word-finding and confrontation naming impairment shared across all three canonical PPA variants, arising from variant-specific lexical-semantic or phonological retrieval breakdown.

evidence.reference_title: Language training for oral and written naming impairment in primary progressive aphasia: a review.
evidence.snippet: Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by a gradual, insidious and progressive loss of language abilities, with naming difficulties being an early and persistent impairment common to all three variants.

evidence.reference_title: A review on primary progressive aphasia.
evidence.snippet: All present with and are characterized by the presence of anomia, and differentiated on the basis of measures of fluency, the presence or absence of logopenia or word finding difficulties, and loss of word meaning or comprehension.

evidence.reference_title: A review on primary progressive aphasia.
evidence.snippet: Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is a neurodegenerative disease of insidious onset presenting with progressive isolated loss of language function, without significant impairment in other cognitive domains.

evidence.reference_title: A review on primary progressive aphasia.
evidence.snippet: Current diagnostic criteria require the language dysfunction to remain isolated for at least two years, and to remain the salient feature as the disease progresses, usually to involve other domains such as behavior, executive functions, and judgment.

nodes.description: Misfolded pathogenic proteins—most commonly TDP-43 in semantic variant PPA, hyperphosphorylated tau in nonfluent/agrammatic PPA, or Alzheimer disease amyloid-beta and tau pathology in logopenic PPA—accumulate within left-hemisphere language-associated cortical regions.
nodes.id: Cortical Proteinopathy Accumulation in Language Regions

evidence.reference_title: Clinicoradiological and neuropathological evaluation of primary progressive aphasia
evidence.snippet: Three PPA variants correlate with distinct underlying pathologies: semantic variant PPA (svPPA) with transactive response DNA-binding protein of 43 kD (TDP-43) proteinopathy, agrammatic variant PPA (agPPA) with tau deposition and logopenic variant PPA (lvPPA) with Alzheimer’s disease (AD).

nodes.description: Microstructural degeneration of major perisylvian and temporoparietal white matter tracts—including the superior longitudinal fasciculus (dorsal stream) and the inferior longitudinal and uncinate fasciculi (ventral stream)—disconnects frontal, insular, temporal, and parietal language nodes.
nodes.id: Dorsal and Ventral White Matter Language Tract Disconnection

evidence.reference_title: White matter damage in primary progressive aphasias: a diffusion tensor tractography study.
evidence.snippet: The most prominent white matter changes were found in the dorsal pathways in non-fluent patients, in the two ventral pathways and the temporal components of the dorsal pathways in semantic variant, and in the temporoparietal component of the dorsal bundles in logopenic patients.

nodes.description: Asymmetric neuronal and synaptic degeneration produces focal gray matter atrophy in left-hemisphere language cortices, preferentially involving the left posterior frontoinsular cortex (including Broca area) in nonfluent/agrammatic PPA, the anterior temporal lobe in semantic PPA, and the left temporoparietal junction (including Wernicke area) in logopenic PPA.

evidence.reference_title: White matter damage in primary progressive aphasias: a diffusion tensor tractography study.
evidence.snippet: These clinical entities have been associated with characteristic patterns of focal grey matter atrophy in left posterior frontoinsular, anterior temporal and left temporoparietal regions, respectively.

evidence.reference_title: Primary Progressive Aphasia.
evidence.snippet: In PPA, neuroanatomical changes primarily affect brain regions associated with language processing. The specific areas vary depending on the PPA subtype, but commonly involved brain regions affect left-hemisphere language functions.

nodes.description: Impaired repetition of sentences and phrases accompanied by word-finding pauses in spontaneous speech without frank agrammatism or loss of single-word comprehension, defining logopenic variant PPA.

evidence.reference_title: Language training for oral and written naming impairment in primary progressive aphasia: a review.
evidence.snippet: l/phvPPA has core features of deficits in word retrieval and sentence repetition [6].

nodes.description: Progressive loss of single-word comprehension and semantic object knowledge, most pronounced initially for low-frequency and low-familiarity items, defining semantic variant PPA alongside severe anomia.

evidence.reference_title: Language training for oral and written naming impairment in primary progressive aphasia: a review.
evidence.snippet: svPPA is clinically characterized by a slow loss of semantic knowledge ... anomia, and single-word comprehension deficits, especially for low-frequency items

evidence.reference_title: A review on primary progressive aphasia.
evidence.snippet: The semantic variant is characterized by fluent, grammatically correct speech, loss of word and object meaning, surface dyslexia and relatively preserved syntactic comprehension skills.

nodes.description: Neurodegenerative processes selectively affect language networks, producing regional cortical FDG-PET hypometabolism (represented functionally by decreased cortical glucose metabolism) and progressive loss of language comprehension, word retrieval, sentence repetition, and grammar/speech production with initial sparing of non-language cognitive domains.

evidence.reference_title: A review on primary progressive aphasia.
evidence.snippet: Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is a neurodegenerative disease of insidious onset presenting with progressive isolated loss of language function, without significant impairment in other cognitive domains.

evidence.reference_title: FDG-PET in the diagnosis of primary progressive aphasia: a systematic review
evidence.snippet: The three PPA subtypes show distinct regions of hypometabolism in FDG-PET imaging with SD in the anterior temporal lobes, LPA in the left temporo-parietal junction, and nonfluent/agrammatic Variant PPA (nfvPPA) in the left inferior frontal gyrus and insula.

nodes.description: Impaired motor speech planning and programming accompanying agrammatic primary progressive aphasia, particularly in 4R-tauopathy cases.

evidence.reference_title: Clinicoradiological and neuropathological evaluation of primary progressive aphasia
evidence.snippet: Apraxia of speech was associated with 4R-tauopathy in agPPA, while pure agrammatic PPA without apraxia was linked to 3R-tauopathy.

evidence.reference_title: Language training for oral and written naming impairment in primary progressive aphasia: a review.
evidence.snippet: As an initial sign of disease, apraxia of speech is frequently recorded [3, 6, 8].

nodes.description: Supportive management with targeted speech-language therapy, communication strategies, counseling, and education for patients and caregivers.

evidence.reference_title: A review on primary progressive aphasia.
evidence.snippet: Referral to specialized centers where speech therapy, counseling, and education for both patient and caregiver are available may be helpful.

nodes.description: Impaired reading of orthographically irregular words (regularization errors) accompanying semantic variant PPA.

evidence.reference_title: Language training for oral and written naming impairment in primary progressive aphasia: a review.
evidence.snippet: Patients with svPPA are fluent in spontaneous speech and word repetition is spared, although they can exhibit surface dyslexia and dysgraphia [3, 6, 12].
